text.en: FADE IN:

A small kitchen, warm with the smell of fresh bread. MOTHER, 30s, flour to the elbows, kneads dough at a worn table. Her daughter RED, 8, all elbows and impatience, sits swinging her legs from a stool, a red woollen cloak already draped over her shoulders.
Is it ready yet?
(not looking up)
It's ready when it's ready. Same as yesterday, and the day before that.
Grandmother's bread is always ready faster.
Grandmother has had sixty more years of practice than you have patience.
Red grins and hops down to peer into the covered BASKET waiting on the sideboard - a fresh loaf, a jar of honey, a twist of butter, a small paper packet of tea.
Can I bring her the good tea? The one in the tin with the birds on it?
(smiling, relenting)
Go on, then. But wrap it well - that tin rattles like a startled goose.
Red fetches the tin, wraps it in a cloth, and tucks it carefully into the basket beside the loaf. Mother wipes her hands on her apron and crosses to tie the cloak's ribbon snug at Red's throat.
Now. Straight there and straight back. Promise me.
I promise.
Grandmother hasn't been well. Give her the basket, sit with her a while, mind your manners, and do not stop to talk to strangers on the way.
(already halfway out the door)
Not even the friendly ones?
Especially the friendly ones. The unfriendly ones are easy enough to spot.
Red laughs, kisses her mother's floury cheek, and is gone, the basket swinging from one arm.
Mother stands in the doorway, watching Red skip down the lane toward the tree line, until she's out of sight past the well.
A WOODCUTTER, broad and unhurried, passes on the road with an axe over one shoulder, and tips his cap.
Morning. Sending the little one off alone again?
She knows the path better than I do most days. Straight to her grandmother's and no further.
I'll be working the near stand of pines past noon, if she needs a familiar face along the way.
(grateful)
That's kind of you.
He nods and continues on toward the forest, whistling.
Tall pines, sunlight breaking through in long gold bars. Red walks the path at an unhurried pace, humming to herself, swinging the basket in wide arcs.
She stops at a cluster of wildflowers at the path's edge - white, blue, one stubborn yellow bloom - and crouches to consider them.
(to herself)
Grandmother likes the blue ones best.
She picks a small handful, tucking them alongside the tin in the basket. Somewhere off in the trees, a bird calls twice and falls silent.
A WOLF steps out from behind a wide trunk a little further up the path, unhurried, almost polite, his manner more curious than threatening.
Good morning, little one. That's a fine basket for such a small pair of arms.
(not especially alarmed)
It's for my grandmother. She's unwell.
Unwell. How sad to hear. Bread, is it, under that cloth? And something in a tin, by the sound of it.
Bread, honey, butter, and her favourite tea. And flowers, now.
A thoughtful girl. And where might I find this fortunate grandmother, if I wished to send my sympathies along with yours?
Past the mill, along the stream, the little cottage with the blue door and the crooked chimney.
(already turning to go)
Then I hope she feels better soon. Mind the roots along the stream bank - they catch the unwary.
I know this path. I've walked it a hundred times.
(a small, private smile)
I'm sure you have.
The Wolf slips off the path at an easy trot, angling through the underbrush toward the mill. Red, already distracted by a second cluster of flowers, doesn't watch him go.
Red picks her way across flat stones at a shallow crossing, basket held high, tongue between her teeth in concentration. On the far bank, she pauses to watch a family of ducks paddle past.
(calling after them)
You're going the wrong way for supper.
She laughs at her own joke and continues on, unhurried, the cottage still some distance off.

A modest, tidy bedroom. GRANDMOTHER, frail but sharp-eyed, sits propped against pillows with a shawl around her shoulders, a half-finished piece of knitting in her lap. The blue door, out of sight down the hall, creaks open.
(calling out)
Is that the Woodcutter's boy with the firewood?
No answer. A shadow crosses the hallway floorboards, unhurried.
(less certain now)
Who's there?
The shadow reaches the bedroom doorway. Grandmother's knitting needles go still in her hands.
A long beat. Then the wardrobe door across the room swings shut with a soft click.
Silence returns to the cottage - too complete a silence for a house that was occupied a moment ago.
The quilt shifts. A large shape now lies where Grandmother sat, a nightcap pulled low over unfamiliar eyes, the shawl arranged just so.
From the front of the cottage, a door opens.
Grandmother? It's me. I've brought bread, and honey, and your birds tin.
Red steps inside, sets the basket on the kitchen table, and pauses at the unnatural quiet of the house.
Grandmother?
(muffled, from the bedroom, gruff)
In here, dear. I've caught a chill - stay by the door a moment.
Red frowns, but crosses toward the bedroom anyway, the flowers still in one hand.
Red stops in the doorway. The shape under the quilt watches her through slitted eyes, nightcap low, shawl pulled close.
(uncertain)
You sound different today.
(a strained, careful voice)
The chill. It does terrible things to a voice.
(approaching, cautious now)
Grandmother, what big ears you have.
All the better to hear you with, my dear.
Grandmother, what big eyes you have.
All the better to see you with, in this dim little room.
(stopping at the bedside, very still now)
Grandmother, what big teeth you have.
(the shawl slipping)
All the better to -
The quilt is flung back. Red doesn't wait to hear the rest - she's already backing toward the door, then running, the flowers scattering across the floorboards behind her.
Red bursts out the blue door, calling out for help. Down the lane, the WOODCUTTER looks up from a fallen log at the sound and breaks into a run, axe still in hand.
What's happened? Are you hurt?
(pointing back at the cottage)
Inside - it isn't Grandmother, it isn't -
Stay behind me.
He strides past her and shoulders through the blue door.

The Wolf freezes halfway out of the bed, caught between the quilt and the window, which is shut fast. The wardrobe door swings open on its own to reveal Grandmother, entirely unharmed, wrapped in a spare blanket she'd hidden herself in, brandishing a rolling pin with both hands.
Out. Now. Before I decide the pin isn't punishment enough.
The Wolf doesn't need telling twice. He scrambles past the Woodcutter, who steps neatly aside rather than test his luck with an axe indoors, and is gone out the window in a single ungainly leap.
The Wolf tears off across the meadow and does not look back. Red watches from the doorway, still catching her breath, as Grandmother appears behind her, blanket over one shoulder like a queen's cape.
(dryly)
Well. That's one way to start a visit.
(half laughing, half shaking)
I brought the tea.
Then let's have some. I find I need it rather badly.
The Woodcutter retrieves the scattered flowers from the bedroom floor and hands them back to Red with a small bow, as if returning something valuable rather than a little worse for the excitement.
I believe these are yours.
(taking them)
Thank you. For coming, I mean. Not just the flowers.
Anytime this path needs minding, I'm not far off.
Grandmother pours tea from the rescued tin into two chipped cups. Red sits across from her, the empty basket on the floor beside her chair, flowers now in a jar of water on the windowsill.
Your mother will want the whole story, and she will not enjoy a single word of it.
Do I have to tell her about talking to him on the path?
(a knowing look over her cup)
You do. And you'll tell her you won't do it again, and you'll mean it this time.
I will. I promise. Properly, this time.
See that you do. Grandmothers only have so many rolling pins in them.
Red walks home along the same path, the empty basket swinging from one arm, already rehearsing how she'll tell the story - faster each time she practises it, and no less true for the speed.
FADE OUT.
